     USA v. Parse


 1                                UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS

 2                                      FOR THE SECOND CIRCUIT

 3                                                   ------

 4                                             August Term, 2014

 5                     (Argued: October 16, 2014              Decided: June 8, 2015)

 6                                            Docket No. 13-1388

 7   _________________________________________________________

 8   UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,

 9                                                          Appellee,

10                                          - v. -

11   DAVID PARSE,

12                                                          Defendant-Appellant.

13   _________________________________________________________

14   Before: KEARSE, STRAUB, and WESLEY, Circuit Judges.

15                  Appeal from a judgment of conviction entered in the United States District Court for

16   the Southern District of New York, William H. Pauley III, Judge, following a trial at which the jury

17   found defendant guilty of mail fraud, in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 1341 and 2, and attempting to

18   interfere with the administration of the federal tax laws, in violation of 26 U.S.C. § 7212(a), and found

19   some of his codefendants guilty of those and other tax-related offenses. Defendant contends

20   principally that the district court--which, pursuant to Fed. R. Crim. P. 33 granted a new trial to his

21   codefendants on the ground of juror misconduct where one of the jurors had lied on voir dire, had
  1   deliberately concealed relevant information about herself, her family, and her past, and was found to

 2   have been actually biased against the defendants--erred in denying defendant's Rule 33 motion on the

 3   basis that defendant had waived his right to an unbiased jury. See United States v. Daugerdas, 867

 4   F.Supp.2d 445 (S.D.N.Y. 2012).

 5                  Vacated and remanded.

 6                  Judge Straub, in a separate opinion, concurs in the judgment and in the majority

 7   opinion in part.

 8                          STANLEY J. OKULA, JR., Assistant United States Attorney, New
 9                               York, New York (Preet Bharara, United States Attorney for the
10                               Southern District of New York, Brian A. Jacobs, Assistant
11                               United States Attorney, Nanette L. Davis, Special Assistant
12                               United States Attorney, New York, New York, on the brief),
13                               for Appellee.

14                          ALEXANDRA A.E. SHAPIRO, New York, New York (Marc E.
15                              Isserles, James Darrow, Chetan A. Patil, Shapiro, Arato &
16                              Isserles, New York, New York, on the brief), for Defendant-
17                              Appellant.

18                          Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher, New York, New York (Lawrence J.
19                                Zweifach, Jane Kim, of counsel), and Arnold & Porter, New
20                                York, New York (Craig A. Stewart, Alexandra L. Mitter, of
21                                counsel), filed a brief for Amicus Curiae New York Council of
22                                Defense Lawyers, in support of Defendant-Appellant.


23   KEARSE, Circuit Judge:

24                  Defendant David Parse appeals from a judgment entered in the United States District

25   Court for the Southern District of New York following a jury trial before William H. Pauley III, Judge,

26   convicting him on one count of mail fraud, in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 1341 and 2, and on one count

27   of corruptly endeavoring to obstruct and impede the administration of the internal revenue laws, in



                                                       2
  1   violation of 26 U.S.C. § 7212(a). Parse was sentenced principally to 42 months' imprisonment, to be

 2   followed by three years of supervised release, and was ordered to forfeit $1,000,000 and to pay

 3   $115,830,267 in restitution. On appeal, he contends principally that he should have been granted a

 4   new trial on the ground of newly discovered evidence of juror bias; he challenges the district court's

 5   denial of his posttrial motion pursuant to Rule 33 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure for that

 6   relief, made jointly with his codefendants against whom the jury had returned verdicts of guilty, in

 7   light of postverdict evidence establishing that one of the jurors had lied on voir dire, concealed

 8   relevant information, and was actually biased against the defendants. The district court granted the

 9   new-trial motion of Parse's codefendants; but it denied the motion of Parse, finding that his attorneys

10   either knew of the juror's misconduct prior to the verdict or failed to act with reasonable diligence

11   based on the information they had, and that Parse had thus waived his right to an impartial jury. Parse

12   also contends that the evidence was insufficient to support the jury's verdicts against him, and he

13   challenges certain of the instructions given to the jury. Finding merit in Parse's challenge to the denial

14   of his Rule 33 motion, but not in his sufficiency challenges, we vacate the judgment and remand for

15   a new trial of the counts on which Parse was convicted.



16                                             I. BACKGROUND



17                   Parse and several others were indicted in 2009 and were ultimately charged with one

18   count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to commit mail fraud, wire fraud, and tax

19   evasion, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 371, and with multiple substantive counts of tax evasion and other

20   tax-related offenses in connection with the creation of a series of tax shelters "designed and marketed


                                                         3
  1   by [a law firm and an accounting firm] to take advantage of Internal Revenue Code . . . loopholes so

 2   taxpayers could claim non-economic tax losses to avoid taxes they otherwise would have owed" (Parse

 3   brief on appeal at 7). Parse was a broker employed by an investment banking firm that executed

 4   transactions for implementation of the shelters.

 5                   In the spring of 2011, Parse was tried along with four of his codefendants: Paul

 6   Daugerdas and Donna Guerin, who were attorneys at the law firm; Denis Field, a member of the

 7   accounting firm; and Craig Brubaker, a broker at the investment bank that employed Parse. Following

 8   a three-month trial at which 41 witnesses testified and some 1,300 exhibits were admitted, the jury on

 9   May 24 returned a split verdict. It found Parse guilty on two counts--the substantive mail fraud and

10   obstruction charges described above--and found him not guilty on the other four counts against him.

11   (See Trial Transcript ("Tr.") 9153-54, 9159-63.) It found Daugerdas guilty on all 24 counts against

12   him; found Guerin guilty on all 12 counts against her; found Field guilty on all 7 counts against him;

13   and found Brubaker not guilty on any of the counts against him. (See id. at 9153-63.)



14   A. The District Court's Findings of Juror Misconduct

15                   In July 2011, Parse, Daugerdas, Guerin, and Field moved pursuant to Fed. R. Crim. P.

16   33(a) for a new trial on the ground that one of the jurors, Catherine M. Conrad--"Juror No. 1" (or

17   "Conrad")--had lied and withheld material information during voir dire and was biased against

18   defendants. The motion was made some two weeks after the government disclosed to defendants and

19   the district judge a letter it had received from Conrad shortly after the return of the verdict. (See Part

20   I.A.2. below.) Following completion of the parties' submissions on the motion, including information

21   from Parse's attorneys as to their earlier suspicions about Conrad (see Part I.B. below) and an


                                                         4
  1   evidentiary hearing, the district court, in a thorough opinion, see United States v. Daugerdas, 867

 2   F.Supp.2d 445 (S.D.N.Y. 2012) ("Daugerdas"), found it "undisputed that Conrad lied extensively

 3   during voir dire and concealed important information about her background," id. at 451. The district

 4   court's description of the voir dire proceedings concerning Conrad and the information about her that

 5   was unearthed in Parse's attorneys' investigations, as to which there is no material dispute, included

 6   the following.



 7          1. Conrad's Voir Dire

 8                    For jury selection, an initial venire of 450 prospective jurors had been assembled; "the

 9   Jury Department provided counsel with a jury roll identifying the prospective jurors in the venire, and

10   listing a 'Catherine M. Conrad' with a Bronxville residence." Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 449.

11   Preliminary procedures winnowed the number of prospective jurors from 450 to approximately 175;

12   the panel of 175 was sworn in for voir dire. In discussing defendants' new-trial motion, the district

13   court stated, quoting the transcript of the voir dire proceedings, that the court had

14                    posed a number of questions to the panel as a whole, including five that are
15                    relevant to this motion:

16                                   1. "Do any of you know or have you had any association,
17                           professional, business, social, direct or indirect, with any member of
18                           the staff of the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District
19                           of New York, the United States Department of Justice, or the Internal
20                           Revenue Service? Has anybody had any dealings with the U.S.
21                           Attorney's Office, the Department of Justice, or the IRS?" (Trial
22                           Tr. 84-85.)

23                                   2. "Are you or [has] any member of your family ever been a
24                           party to [a] lawsuit, that is, a plaintiff or a defendant in a civil case or
25                           a criminal case?" (Trial Tr. 105.)



                                                          5
  1                                  3. "Have any of you or a close relative ever been involved or
 2                          appeared as a witness in any investigation by a federal or state grand
 3                          jury or any congressional committees or state legislative bodies or
 4                          licensing authorities or planning boards?" (Trial Tr. 107.)

 5                                 4. "Have any of you ever been a witness or a complainant in
 6                          any hearing or trial, whether it be in the state or federal courts?" (Trial
 7                          Tr. 108.)

 8                                 5. "[H]ave you or any member of your family or any very close
 9                          personal friend ever been arrested or charged with a crime?" (Trial
10                          Tr. 118.)

11                          Conrad responded affirmatively to only two of these questions. In
12                  response to the first question, Conrad offered that her father "works for DOJ
13                  across the street" as "an immigration officer." (Trial Tr. 85.) She then assured
14                  this Court that his position would not affect her ability to be fair and impartial.
15                  (Trial Tr. 85.) In response to the second question, Conrad stated that she "was
16                  a plaintiff in a personal injury negligence case . . . pending" in Bronx Supreme
17                  Court. (Trial Tr. 105.) Again, she represented that her personal injury action
18                  would not interfere with her ability to serve as a juror. (Trial Tr. 106.) Conrad
19                  did not provide any additional information or any other affirmative answers to
20                  questions posed to the group.

21   Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 449-50 (emphases ours).

22                  The district court had proceeded to ask further, more detailed, questions of the

23   prospective jurors individually.

24                         THE COURT: . . . . Ms. Conrad . . . . would you tell us what
25                  neighborhood you reside in?

26                          CONRAD: Bronx Village [sic] [Bronxville] in Westchester.

27                          THE COURT: How long have you lived at your current address?

28                          CONRAD: My whole life.

29                          ....

30                          THE COURT: Do you work outside the home?



                                                        6
  1                          CONRAD: No. I'm a stay-at-home wife.

 2                          ....

 3                          THE COURT: . . . . What is the highest level of education you've
 4                  attained?

 5                         CONRAD: I have a BA in English literature [and] classics, and I
 6                  studied archeology abroad.

 7   Id. at 450-51 (quoting voir dire transcript at 203-04 (emphases ours)). The court noted that it had

 8   offered prospective jurors the opportunity to come to the bench for a sidebar with respect to any

 9   information that they preferred not to give publicly. Several prospective jurors took advantage of that

10   offer, but Conrad sought no such sidebar and provided no other information in response to these

11   questions. See id. at 450.

12                  The court found that Conrad in voir dire had lied about, among other matters, her own

13   background and that of her husband.

14                          Conrad lied about her educational, professional, and personal
15                  background. While she informed the Court that her highest level of education
16                  was a bachelor's degree, she in fact obtained her juris doctorate from Brooklyn
17                  Law School in 1997 and was admitted to practice law in New York in January
18                  2000. . . . Further, although she informed the Court that she was a "stay-at-
19                  home wife," she had practiced law for some time until the New York Supreme
20                  Court Appellate Division, First Department (the "Appellate Division")
21                  suspended her law license. . . . And the day before she was sworn as a
22                  prospective juror, she sought to have her law license reinstated. Conrad
23                  answered under oath that she owned a home and lived in Bronxville in
24                  Westchester County "all my life." (Trial Tr. at 203.) That, too, was a lie. In
25                  fact, Conrad rented an apartment and lived on Barker Avenue in the Bronx for
26                  years.

27   Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 452 (emphases ours); see also id. at 458 (finding that on the juror

28   qualification questionnaire completed under oath prior to voir dire, Conrad "lied" in stating that "her

29   permanent address was in Bronxville, New York," thereby enabling her to collect "collect[] an


                                                       7
  1   additional $765 in travel expenses based on her use of a Westchester zip code").

 2                  As to the concealment by Conrad of the fact that she had been educated as and

 3   practiced as an attorney, the court noted that

 4                          Conrad also hid the fact that she was the subject of an investigation and
 5                  disciplinary proceedings conducted by the Departmental Disciplinary
 6                  Committee (the "Disciplinary Committee") of the Appellate Division. In
 7                  December 2007, the Appellate Division suspended Conrad from the practice
 8                  of law for failing "to cooperate with the [Disciplinary] Committee's
 9                  investigation into two complaints alleging professional misconduct which
10                  threatens the public interest." In the Matter of Catherine M. Conrad ("2007
11                  Suspension Order"), 48 A.D.3d 187, 188, 846 N.Y.S.2d 912 (1st Dep't 2007).
12                  According to one complaint, Conrad "violated court orders and failed to appear
13                  as directed, ultimately resulting in the dismissal of the action." 2007
14                  Suspension Order, 48 A.D.3d at 188, 846 N.Y.S.2d 912. According to the
15                  second complaint, she failed to oppose an order to show cause, resulting in an
16                  adverse ruling against her client. 2007 Suspension Order, 48 A.D.3d at 188,
17                  846 N.Y.S.2d 912. In response to her state bar suspension, on January 4, 2008,
18                  Conrad was suspended from the bar of the United States District Court for the
19                  Southern District of New York. See In re Catherine M. Conrad, No. M-2-238
20                  (JSR) (S.D.N.Y. Jan. 4, 2008); see also Local Civ. Rule 1.5(b)(5) (violations
21                  of the New York State Rules of Professional Conduct are grounds for
22                  discipline, including suspension). On January 29, 2008, Conrad was
23                  suspended from the bar of the United States District Court for the Eastern
24                  District of New York. See In re Catherine M. Conrad, No. MC-08-010 (BMC)
25                  (E.D.N.Y. Jan. 29, 2008).

26   Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 453. With respect to the fact that Conrad was seeking to practice law

27   again, the court found that her "application for reinstatement," filed on the day before voir dire began,

28                  was riddled with falsehoods. She failed to report that she had not paid a fine
29                  imposed on her by the Eastern District of New York, even though the
30                  application required that disclosure. (See . . . Letter from Chief Counsel Jorge
31                  Dopico of the Disciplinary Committee, dated Aug. 9, 2011 ("Dopico Letter"),
32                  at 3.) She also stated, in response to a direct question on the application, that
33                  she had not used any other names, even though she had used the name
34                  "Catherine Rosa" when arrested in May 2009. (Dopico Letter, at 5). Finally,
35                  she stated that she had no arrests or convictions since her suspension in 2007,
36                  when in fact she had pleaded guilty to shoplifting charges in October 2009.
37                  (Dopico Letter, at 5.)


                                                        8
  1   Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 454.

 2                  The court went on to recount other instances of Conrad's misrepresentations as to her

 3   criminal history:

 4                  According to New York and Arizona criminal records, Conrad was arrested
 5                  and charged with crimes on at least five occasions. . . .

 6                          On April 17, 1998, Conrad was arrested in New York and charged with
 7                  driving while intoxicated, reckless endangerment, leaving the scene of an
 8                  accident, assault, resisting arrest, and harassment. . . . On October 21, 1998,
 9                  she pleaded guilty to the misdemeanor driving while intoxicated charge. . . .
10                  Shortly before that plea, on September 23, 1998, she was arrested again and
11                  charged with criminal contempt and aggravated harassment. She pleaded
12                  guilty to these misdemeanors on May 17, 1999, and was sentenced to three
13                  years probation. . . .

14                          On August 4, 2007, Conrad was arrested in Arizona for disorderly
15                  conduct. . . . At approximately 5:00 a.m., local police responded to a call from
16                  Conrad, complaining of a domestic dispute at a motel with Rosa, who she had
17                  married six weeks earlier. . . . As the police investigated, she was highly
18                  disruptive, disturbed other hotel guests, and ignored the responding officers'
19                  requests to quiet down. Ultimately, the officers placed Conrad under arrest and
20                  booked her at the Navajo County Jail on charges of disorderly conduct. On
21                  August 7, 2007, Conrad was released on her own recognizance and ordered to
22                  appear for arraignment on August 14. . . . She failed to appear and an arrest
23                  warrant was issued. . . . It appears that warrant remains outstanding.

24                          In May 2009, Conrad was arrested in New York on two separate
25                  occasions for shoplifting. . . . On May 6, she was arrested for shoplifting $47
26                  worth of groceries from a Yonkers supermarket. . . . Days later, on May 14,
27                  she was arrested again for shoplifting approximately $27 worth of goods from
28                  a New Rochelle supermarket. . . . Both charges were resolved by a plea to a
29                  single count of petit larceny. . . . Under her plea agreement, Conrad was placed
30                  on probation for three years. . . . A July 14 probation report noted that Conrad
31                  was in an outpatient treatment program for alcoholism. . . . An October
32                  probation report indicated that the outpatient program expelled her because of
33                  her continued use of alcohol and recommended a four-week inpatient
34                  program. . . . While it is unclear whether she participated in that program,
35                  Conrad was on probation during voir dire and throughout the entire trial of this
36                  case.



                                                       9
  1   Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 454-55 (emphases added).

 2                   In Conrad's voir dire, she had been asked whether there were other members of her

 3   household and had responded that she lived with her husband, whom she described as being retired.

 4   When the court asked "What is he retired from?" Conrad responded, "He owns some bus companies."

 5   Id. at 450 (internal quotation marks omitted). The district court found that in fact "Conrad's husband,

 6   Frank J. Rosa ('Rosa'), is a career criminal," id. at 454, and that her response was a "fabrication . . .

 7   designed to conceal his criminal past," id. at 455:

 8                   According to public records, from 1980 through the late 1990s, Rosa was
 9                   convicted of at least nine criminal offenses. . . . Among other crimes, he was
10                   convicted of receiving stolen property, criminal contempt, possession of a
11                   controlled substance, forgery, and illegal possession of a firearm. . . . He has
12                   been incarcerated on numerous occasions and served a seven year sentence in
13                   Northern State Prison in New Jersey.

14   Id.



15           2. Conrad's Posttrial Letter to the Government

16                   The jury's verdict in the present case was returned on May 24, 2011. On May 25, 2011,

17   Conrad wrote a letter to the Assistant United States Attorney who led the government's trial team (the

18   "May Letter"), praising its performance at trial but lamenting the acquittals of Parse. The district court

19   described the letter as follows:

20                           Conrad authored a two-page type-written letter dated May 25, 2011 to
21                   Assistant United States Attorney Stanley J. Okula, Jr. ("Okula") praising the
22                   Government's prosecution of the case (the "May Letter"). The May Letter was
23                   postmarked May 28. On June 22, the Government forwarded the May Letter
24                   to the Court and defense counsel. . . . In her letter, Conrad wrote, "I thought
25                   that you [i.e., Okula], Ms. Davis and Mr. Hernandez [other members of the
26                   Government's trial team] did an outstanding job on behalf of Our
27                   Government." In describing the jury's role, she stated that "I did feel that we


                                                        10
  1                  reached a fair and just verdict based on the case, facts and evidence presented
 2                  to us." She further explained that "we did have qualms with Mr. David Parse.
 3                  I solely held out for two days on the conspiracy charge for him I wanted to
 4                  convict 100%, (not only on that charge)--but on Tuesday, May 24, 2011, we
 5                  had asked for the Judge's clarification of 'willfully' and 'knowingly', I believe,
 6                  and I had to throw in the towel." Conrad went on for an additional two
 7                  paragraphs discussing the strengths and weaknesses of the Government's case
 8                  against Parse, the effectiveness of expert witness testimony, the persuasiveness
 9                  of certain evidence, and the credibility of fact witnesses. She concluded her
10                  letter by writing, "I have learned, the saying a 'federal case' is REALLY a
11                  'federal case', and I feel privileged to have had the opportunity to observe la
12                  creme de la creme--KUDOS to you and your team!!!"

13   Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 452 (capitalization in May Letter) (italics ours). (See also May Letter

14   at 2 ("Mr. Parse presented a conundrum--not for me, but for the other eleven.").)

15                  Defendants' motion for a new trial stated that Conrad's May Letter had prompted them

16   to investigate Conrad and that they thereby learned of her disciplinary proceedings and her status as

17   a suspended lawyer by searching public records. The court eventually scheduled an evidentiary

18   hearing with respect to Conrad's conduct (see Part I.A.3. below) and with respect to the timing of the

19   parties' knowledge of her misconduct (see Part I.B. below).



20          3. The Evidentiary Hearings on Conrad's Conduct

21                  The evidentiary hearing was scheduled for February 15-16, 2012. In the meantime, the

22   court ordered Conrad to appear in person on December 20, 2011--with the parties agreeing to

23   participate by telephone--in order for the court to instruct Conrad as to her constitutional rights and

24   to appoint an attorney for her if she could not afford one:

25                  The Court directed the U.S. Marshals to serve Conrad with a copy of the order
26                  to appear. The marshals served Conrad at her apartment in the Bronx, and on
27                  receiving the order, she stated, "I think I know what this is about, I failed to
28                  disclose that I'm a lawyer, but they never asked, so I didn't lie." Conrad


                                                       11
  1                  recognized a photograph of herself that the marshals carried and said, "that
 2                  picture must be from my rap sheet." (GX 3500-2, U.S. Marshals Report dated
 3                  Dec. 16, 2011.)

 4   Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 455. At the December hearing,

 5                  Conrad advised the Court that there was no reason for an evidentiary hearing
 6                  because, in her view "[Defendants are] fricken crooks and they should be in jail
 7                  and you know that." (12/20 Tr. 17.) She went on to opine: "come on, this is
 8                  anything in favor of the defendants. . . . And they brought the motion against
 9                  the prosecution . . . . It's ridiculous." (12/20 Tr. 17.)

10   Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 455-56.

11                  On February 15, 2012, Conrad refused to present herself at the evidentiary hearing.

12   She attended only after the court issued a warrant for her immediate arrest, and the U.S. Marshals took

13   her into custody and brought her to court. See id. at 475. At the February hearing ("Hearing" or

14   "Hr'g"), Conrad invoked her Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination but, on motion of

15   the government, was granted use immunity. See id. at 456 n.2 (immunity from use of her "testimony

16   or other information compelled under this Order, or any information directly or indirectly derived from

17   such testimony or other information, . . . except a prosecution for perjury, giving a false statement, or

18   otherwise failing to comply with this Order." (internal quotation marks omitted)).

19                           At the Hearing, Conrad admitted that she lied to the Court to make
20                  herself more "marketable" as a juror. . . . She also testified that she believed
21                  that if the truth were known, "the defense counsel would be wild to have me"
22                  on the jury. . . . Conrad reasoned that Defendants would want "crooks" on the
23                  jury because they themselves were "crooks." . . . . Indeed, Conrad admitted
24                  that she had used this to rationalize her conduct to herself at the time of voir
25                  dire. (Hr'g Tr. 229 ("Q. You told yourself at the time that it was OK from the
26                  defendants' perspective because, if anything, somebody who was married to a
27                  criminal would tend to favor other criminals, right? A. I guess it can be
28                  characterized as that.").) Conrad acknowledged that she made the conscious
29                  decision to perjure herself between the first and second day of voir dire. After
30                  hearing the questions posed to the first two prospective jurors, she conjured up
31                  a personal profile that she thought would be attractive. . . .


                                                        12
  1                          At the Hearing, Conrad opined that "most attorneys" are "career
 2                  criminals." . . . . Daugerdas and Guerin are attorneys, and while Parse is [sic]
 3                  licensed to practice law, he is an investment banker. She twice underlined the
 4                  difference in financial success between herself and Daugerdas. When asked
 5                  if she had about $14,000 in assets, Conrad retorted: "Correct. Much less than
 6                  your client." . . . . When asked whether she was financially successful as a
 7                  lawyer, Conrad testified: "I don't live an extravagant lifestyle like Mr.
 8                  Daugerdas."

 9   Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 456 (footnote omitted) (emphases and brackets ours).

10                         When given a chance to explain her declaration that all the Defendants
11                  were "crooks" and that their motion for a new trial was "ridiculous," she
12                  claimed repeatedly that she did not recall what she meant to convey. She also
13                  claimed she did not know why she made those statements because "I'm not a
14                  psychologist."

15   Id. Her responses to other inquiries into her past statements were similarly evasive. See id. at 456-57;

16   id. at 457 ("She claimed repeatedly that she could neither understand the questions nor remember the

17   facts.")

18                  The court concluded that Conrad was "a pathological liar and utterly untrustworthy."

19   Id. at 470.

20                          Conrad's lies are breathtaking. In response to direct and unambiguous
21                  questions, she intentionally provided numerous false and misleading answers
22                  and omitted material information. Conrad's lies were calculated to prevent the
23                  Court and the parties from learning her true identity, which would have
24                  prevented her from serving on the jury. This is not a case where the relevant
25                  voir dire questions were somehow vague or ambiguous, particularly given
26                  Conrad's status as an attorney. . . . The Court's questions to Conrad were clear,
27                  simple, and direct.

28                          The events she lied about were recent, personally significant, and
29                  directly affected her qualifications to serve as a juror. Her arrests and
30                  suspensions from the practice of law were not the result of youthful
31                  indiscretions or errors on the part of police or courts. . . . There is no dispute
32                  that Conrad was aware of her prior convictions, her attorney disciplinary
33                  problems, and her personal injury suit at the time she answered the Court's
34                  questions under oath. There is also no question that she made a conscious


                                                       13
  1                  decision to hide them from the Court.

 2   Id. at 468-69 (emphases added). Conrad testified that she knew she could have made nonpublic

 3   disclosures to the court and the attorneys at a sidebar; but she said "'I know my disclosures definitely

 4   would not have allowed me to sit as a juror.'" Id. at 469 (quoting Hr'g Tr. 237). The court concluded

 5   that Conrad's answers concealing material facts were attributable neither to a desire to avoid

 6   embarrassment nor to honest mistakes:

 7                  They were deliberate and intentional lies. Conrad confessed that she
 8                  purposefully lied and omitted material information in her voir dire testimony
 9                  to make herself more "marketable" as a juror. She yearned for professional
10                  redemption or some psychic satisfaction: "And having been suspended for so
11                  long, I guess mentally I would think maybe I'm back in the swing of things
12                  now." (Hr'g Tr. 236.) It is evident that Conrad's untruthful responses to the
13                  Court's voir dire questions were premeditated and deliberate. There is no
14                  innocent explanation.

15   Daugerdas, 867 F.Supp.2d at 469.

16                    The court found "that Conrad was actually biased against Defendants." Id. at 471.

17   It also observed that

18                           Conrad's May Letter to Okula buttresses the conclusion that she was
19                  actually biased. Written the day after the trial concluded, the May Letter
20                  indicates that Conrad identified with the Government. She expressed that bias
21                  in her emphasis on "Our Government"--a phrase she could not explain. (Hr'g
22                  Tr. at 202.) Her bias also bled through when she wrote that she "did fight the
23                  good fight" against acquitting Parse on any counts but eventually had to "throw
24                  in the towel." Her choice of words shows that Conrad saw herself not as a
25                  fact-finder, but as a partisan for "Our Government." In addition, Conrad
26                  included her cell phone number in the return address of the May Letter, and she
27                  testified that she was "very anxious" to talk to the prosecutors after the verdict.
28                  (Hr'g Tr. at 194.) By contrast, she testified that there was "no reason" for her

14                   Rule 33 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure provides, in pertinent part, that

15   "[u]pon the defendant's motion, the court may vacate any judgment and grant a new trial if the interest

16   of justice so requires." Fed. R. Crim. P. 33(a). Such a motion, if made within three years after the

17   verdict or finding of guilty, may be based on "newly discovered evidence," Fed. R. Crim. P. 33(b); but

18   such motions are "not favored," United States v. Diaz, 176 F.3d 52, 106 (2d Cir.) (internal quotation

19   marks omitted), cert. denied, 528 U.S. 875 (1999); United States v. Spencer, 4 F.3d 115, 118 (2d Cir.

 3   v. Mayo, 14 F.3d 128, 132 (2d Cir. 1994) ("Mayo"), and is not considered "newly discovered" if, with

 4   the exercise of reasonable diligence, it could have been discovered before or during the trial, see, e.g.,

 5   United States v. Siddiqi, 959 F.2d 1167, 1173 (2d Cir. 1992) ("Siddiqi") (the defendant must "make[]

 9   impropriety only later if the result of the proceeding is unsatisfactory to him. See generally Puckett

10   v. United States, 556 U.S. 129, 134 (2009) ("If a litigant believes that an error has occurred (to his

 4          1. The Right to an Impartial Jury

 5                  The right of a defendant in a criminal prosecution to a trial "by an impartial jury" is

 6   expressly guaranteed by the Sixth Amendment to the Constitution. U.S. Const. amend VI. "[T]rying

 7   an accused before a jury that is actually biased" not only transgresses the express guarantee of the

 8   Sixth Amendment but also "violates even the most minimal standards of due process." United States

 9   v. Nelson, 277 F.3d 164, 206 (2d Cir.), cert. denied, 537 U.S. 835 (2002); see, e.g., In re Murchison,

10   349 U.S. 133, 136 (1955) ("A fair trial in a fair tribunal is a basic requirement of due process.").

11                  An impartial jury is one in which all of its members, not just most of them, are free of

12   interest and bias. See, e.g., United States v. Martinez-Salazar, 528 U.S. 304, 316 (2000) (an error "in

13   the seating of any juror who should have been dismissed for cause . . . . would require reversal");

14   Parker v. Gladden, 385 U.S. 363, 366 (1966) (per curiam) (despite state law authorizing conviction

15   by an affirmative vote of 10 jurors, a new trial was required where at least two members of the

16   12-person jury were exposed to unauthorized communications; "petitioner was entitled to be tried by

17   12, not 9 or even 10, impartial and unprejudiced jurors").

18                  The voir dire of prospective jurors, who have been placed under oath, "is an important

19   method of protecting a defendant's right to trial by" jurors who are impartial. Colombo, 869 F.2d

20   at 151. A prospective juror who deliberately lies on voir dire is subject to criminal prosecution for

21   perjury pursuant to, e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 1621 ("perjury" includes willfully making a false statement as

12                  Parse and the amicus council of defense lawyers urge us to adopt a general rule that

13   lawyers need not bring concerns about possible juror misconduct--including concerns about possible

14   misstatements made during voir dire--to the attention of the trial court unless counsel actually know

15   that such misconduct has occurred. We doubt that such a sweeping and absolute rule is appropriate;

17   present appeal. Assuming that the district court was correct in its view that Parse's attorneys should

18   have alerted the court to whatever suspicions they had about Conrad prior to the conclusion of the

19   jury's deliberations, we conclude that the improper presence of Conrad on the jury--a forfeited error--

20   warrants plain-error review and warrants reversal under that standard.

21                  Under Fed. R. Crim. P. 52(b), which provides that "[a] plain error that affects

 2                  before an appellate court can correct an error not raised at trial, there must be
 3                  (1) "error," (2) that is "plain," and (3) that "affect[s] substantial rights." . . . .
